content.chapter: Chapter 1: A Plan for a Greener Europe
objectives: Explain what the Green Deal is and when it was announced.
Explain the 2050 aim.
Explain the circular economy.
Use purpose and method forms.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter defines the plan: who announced it, when, its aim and its main idea. A definition map (what → who → when → aim → method) supports learners before the detailed chapters. The circular economy links the topic to daily life.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The European Commission is an EU institution, not a country.
Net zero does not mean no emissions; it means emissions are balanced by what is removed.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: a plan to / its aim is to + verb · by + -ing (method) · in this way
Notice (Activity 1): Its aim is to protect the planet by building a clean economy.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *by build · *a plan for help · *wants fighting.
Use (Activity 4): a circular home.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: sus-TAIN-a-ble, e-CON-o-my, e-MIS-sions, CIR-cu-lar.
Dates: the eleventh of December, twenty nineteen.
beforeReading: Ask: “What does sustainable mean? Give one example.”
duringReading: First reading: What is the Green Deal?
Second reading: complete the definition map.
Find how a circular economy protects nature.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Definition map; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a circular home; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What is the aim of the Green Deal?
How does a circular economy protect nature?
Which parts of life does the plan want to make more eco-friendly?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “11 December 2019” and “Less Waste” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: sustainable, economy, greenhouse gas, emissions, eco-friendly, circular economy.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the definition map with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short dictionary entry for “Green Deal” with one purpose form and one by + -ing.

formativeAssessment: Explains what the Green Deal is.
Explains the circular economy.
Uses purpose or method forms correctly.
expectedResponses: The European Commission announced the Green Deal on 11 December 2019. Its aim is to protect the planet by building a clean economy. In a circular economy, people recycle materials and produce less waste, so nature is protected.
content.transferTask: Write about how your home could be more circular.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners explain the circular economy in their own words?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “Its aim is to … by …-ing”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains what the Green Deal is.

objectives: Explain the three main aims.
Explain the 2030 and 2050 targets.
Explain what Protecting Nature includes.
Use by + amount and by + deadline.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is organized under three headings. A three-column organizer (Climate · Nature · Economy) helps learners sort targets, problems and solutions. The two meanings of “by” are a frequent source of confusion in policy texts.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The 55% target is for 2030; climate neutrality is for 2050.
“By 2030” means not later than 2030, not “in 2030” only.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: reduce by + amount · by + deadline · without + -ing
Notice (Activity 1): … reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *until 2050 (for a deadline) · *without hurt.
Use (Activity 4): my targets.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Numbers: fifty-five percent; twenty thirty; twenty fifty.
Stress: bi-o-di-VER-si-ty, de-for-est-A-tion, neu-TRAL-i-ty.
beforeReading: Ask: “What is the difference between a goal for next year and a goal for 25 years from now?”
duringReading: First reading: What are the three main aims?
Second reading: complete the three-column organizer.
Find the 2030 and 2050 targets.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Three-column organizer; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: my targets; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the chapter call climate neutrality an important step?
What does it mean to benefit from nature responsibly?
How can the economy grow without hurting nature?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “At Least 55%” and “Healthy Land” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: global warming, climate neutrality, deforestation, biodiversity.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the organizer with the three headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph that explains the difference between the 2030 and 2050 targets.

formativeAssessment: Explains the three aims.
Explains the two targets.
Uses both meanings of “by” correctly.
expectedResponses: The EU wants to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030 and reach climate neutrality by 2050. It also wants to stop deforestation and the loss of biodiversity.
content.transferTask: Write about your own green targets.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners separate the 2030 and 2050 targets?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “reduce … by … by …”.

content.chapter: Chapter 3: Why Is the Green Deal Important?
objectives: Explain why the Green Deal is important.
Explain what fossil fuels and net zero are.
Explain the problem of safe energy today.
Use cause and result linkers and the present perfect.
content.pedagogy: The chapter builds an argument: the old way cannot continue, so a net-zero economy is needed; energy is insecure, so the change is urgent. A cause–result chain helps learners follow the argument.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Supply chains are the steps that bring a product to the customer, not only transport.
“For this reason” starts a new sentence; it does not join two clauses like “because”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: because · for this reason · as a result · present perfect (have affected)
Notice (Activity 1): High energy prices … have negatively affected many companies …
Build (Activities 2–3): fill the linkers, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *For this reason that … · *have affect · *As a result of electricity becomes …
Use (Activity 4): effects at home.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: en-vi-ron-MEN-tal, pre-DICT, de-LIV-er-ies, e-lec-TRIC-i-ty.
Linking: as a result /æz ə rɪˈzʌlt/.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why do energy prices go up?”
duringReading: First reading: Why is the Green Deal important?
Second reading: complete the cause–result chain.
Find what wars can do to trade.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Cause–result chain; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: effects at home; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why can we not continue the old ways for long?
Why do many people see a net-zero economy as the key way?
Which industries suffer most from high energy prices?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Serious Danger” and “Supply Chains” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: fossil fuels, net-zero, supply chain.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chain with the first cause written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph that explains the argument of the chapter with three linkers.

formativeAssessment: Explains why the Green Deal is important.
Explains the energy problem.
Uses linkers correctly.
expectedResponses: Old ways of doing business burn too many fossil fuels. For this reason, many people see a net-zero economy as the key way to fight climate change. Wars can block trade routes. As a result, electricity and fuel become expensive.
content.transferTask: Write about how high energy prices affect families.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners follow the argument from cause to result?

exitTicket: Write one cause and one result with “As a result”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why the Green Deal is important.

objectives: Explain why countries are moving to renewable energy.
Explain what industry needs.
Explain why the transition must speed up.
Use so that and should.
content.pedagogy: The chapter answers the problem of Chapter 3 with a solution: renewable energy and a faster transition. A problem–solution chart connects the two chapters.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Renewable energy is “often” cheaper, not always.
“So that” shows purpose; “so” alone often shows a result.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: so that + can (purpose) · should (advice) · quit + -ing
Notice (Activity 1): … must speed up, so that industries can get clean energy …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *quit to depend · *should to make · *money are.
Use (Activity 4): advice for our school.
duringReading: First reading: What are countries moving to?
Second reading: complete the problem–solution chart.
Find what the complete plan should show.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–16 Problem–solution chart; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: advice for our school; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is renewable energy good for countries?
What do countries need to keep industry strong?
Why should the plan show the costs?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Wind and Solar Power” and “A Complete Plan” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: solar power, renewable energy.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the problem from Chapter 3 written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph that links the problem in Chapter 3 with the solution in Chapter 4.

formativeAssessment: Explains why countries use renewable energy.
Explains why the change must be faster.
Uses so that or should correctly.
expectedResponses: More and more countries are moving to renewable energy because it is often cheaper. The transition must speed up, so that industries can get clean energy at a fair price.
content.transferTask: Write advice for a greener school.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners link the solution with the problem in Chapter 3?

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why countries use renewable energy.
Explains why the change must be faster.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: New Opportunities in a Net-Zero Age
objectives: Explain the net-zero age.
Explain which countries can become leaders.
Name the technologies in the Net-Zero Industry Act.
Use will, can and relative clauses.
content.pedagogy: The chapter looks to the future: new markets, new industries and a new law. A future map (markets · technology · jobs · law) helps learners organize the ideas. The technical words are supported by pictures.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Net-Zero Industry Act is an EU law, not a company.
The chapter says some countries “can” lead; it is a possibility, not a fact.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: will (prediction) · can (possibility) · defining relative clauses (that / who / whose)
Notice (Activity 1): Countries that put money into clean technology early …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *will brings · *countries who … (for things it is better to say that) · *can to become.
Use (Activity 4): jobs of the future.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: TUR-bine, SO-lar PAN-el, car-bon di-OX-ide, se-CURE.
Contraction: will → ’ll.
beforeReading: Ask: “What jobs will exist in 2050 that do not exist today?”
duringReading: First reading: What will the net-zero age bring?
Second reading: complete the future map.
Find the technologies in the law.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Future map; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: jobs of the future; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What will the new economy bring?
Why can early investors become leaders?
What does the Net-Zero Industry Act help Europe build?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Net-Zero Age” and “The Net-Zero Industry Act” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: solar panel, carbon dioxide, wind turbine, heat pump.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give picture cards of the five technologies.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short news report about the Net-Zero Industry Act.

formativeAssessment: Explains the net-zero age.
Names the technologies in the law.
Uses will, can or relative clauses correctly.
expectedResponses: In the next 20 or 30 years, a net-zero age will begin. Countries that put money into clean technology early can become world leaders. The Net-Zero Industry Act helps Europe build batteries, wind turbines, heat pumps and solar panels.
content.transferTask: Write about green jobs in your country in the future.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use the technical words correctly?

exitTicket: Write one prediction with “will” and one sentence with “who”.

rubricLevels.secure: Names the technologies in the law.
Uses will, can or relative clauses.

content.chapter: Chapter 6: New Rules for Green Products
objectives: Explain the rule about unsold clothes.
Explain the rule about spare parts.
Explain what factories and governments will do.
Use be allowed to, no longer and will need to.
content.pedagogy: The chapter gives concrete examples of new rules. Learners analyse each rule (who → must / must not → why) and then propose their own rule.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “No longer” means it was possible before; it is not the same as “never”.
The clothes rule is for large companies, not for individuals.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: be (not) allowed to · no longer · will need to
Notice (Activity 1): Large companies … are no longer allowed to destroy clothes …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *are no longer allowed destroy · *will need follow.
Use (Activity 4): a new green rule.
beforeReading: Ask: “What happens to clothes that shops cannot sell?”
duringReading: First reading: What new rules does the chapter give?
Second reading: complete the rule chart.
Find what governments will see as essential.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–16 Rule chart; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a new green rule; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is destroying unsold clothes a problem?
How do spare parts help nature?
What will the rules cover in the future?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “No Longer Allowed” and “Spare Parts” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: spare part.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart: Who? · What is not allowed? · Why?
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph that compares the two rules in the chapter.

formativeAssessment: Explains the two rules.
Explains what factories will need to do.
Uses be allowed to or need to correctly.
expectedResponses: Large companies in the EU are no longer allowed to destroy clothes that they could not sell. Other rules make spare parts easy to find, so people can repair their things.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners give a clear reason for their rule?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “no longer allowed to”.

rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the end of the chapter.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses be allowed to or need to.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: Smart Choices and Green Jobs
objectives: Explain why consumers need clear information.
Explain what energy labels do.
Explain how the job market is changing.
Use depend on, instead of and compete for.
content.pedagogy: The chapter moves from consumers to workers. A two-part organizer (Consumers / Workers) helps learners compare the two sides of the change. Real energy labels make the topic concrete.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Energy labels show energy use; they do not show the price.
“Instead of” is followed by a noun or -ing, not a base verb.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: depend on · instead of · help + person + base verb · compete for
Notice (Activity 1): … the success of the Green Deal depends a lot on people.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *depends of · *instead to buy · *compete to workers.
Use (Activity 4): a smart shopping guide.
beforeReading: Ask: “What do you check before you buy something?”
duringReading: First reading: What do consumers need?
Second reading: complete the two-part organizer.
Find how the job market is changing.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Two-part organizer; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a smart shopping guide; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the success of the Green Deal depend on people?
What should people see before they buy a product?
Why will companies compete for workers?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Energy Labels” and “The Job Market” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: energy label.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a picture of an energy label.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph about the job market with two present perfect sentences.

formativeAssessment: Explains why consumers need information.
Explains how the job market is changing.
Uses the patterns correctly.
expectedResponses: The success of the Green Deal depends a lot on people. Energy labels help people compare products easily. The number of green jobs has grown fast, so large-scale training programs are necessary.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see both sides: consumers and workers?

objectives: Explain why education is a big part of the Green Deal.
Explain why countries should work together.
Explain Türkiye’s Green Deal Action Plan.
Use concluding language.
content.pedagogy: The closing chapter concludes the argument: education and cooperation decide success. Türkiye’s own plan links the text to learners’ country. The jigsaw summit brings the whole book together.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Türkiye’s plan was published in 2021; its net-zero goal is 2053.
“In conclusion” closes a text; it does not start a new topic.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: in conclusion · for this reason · it is helpful for … to · depend on how well
Notice (Activity 1): … will depend mostly on how well countries train workers …
Build (Activities 2–3): fill the linkers, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *In conclusion of · *it is helpful for countries keep · *depend of.
Use (Activity 4): working across borders.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: TÜR-ki-ye.
Numbers: twenty twenty-one; twenty fifty-three.
Stress: com-PET-i-tive, in-ter-NA-tion-al, ed-u-CA-tion.
beforeReading: Ask: “Can one country stop climate change alone?”
duringReading: First reading: What will the success depend on?
Second reading: find who should support the steps.
Find Türkiye’s plan and goal.
afterReading: Group task: “The Green Deal: A Class Summit”.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–16 Who should support; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: working across borders; 42–45 Exit ticket. (Summit in a second lesson.)
discussionPoints: Why does the green change depend on education?
Why is it helpful for countries to work together?
What is Türkiye’s net-zero goal?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Green and Digital Skills” and “Türkiye’s Plan” when the picture is in place.
The jigsaw summit closes the book; give each expert two chapters.
This chapter has no Word Notes.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frame: In conclusion, … For this reason, …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short conclusion for the whole book in four sentences.

formativeAssessment: Explains why education matters.
Explains why countries should work together.
Uses concluding language correctly.
expectedResponses: In conclusion, the success of the green change will depend mostly on education and training. Climate change does not stop at borders, so it is helpful for countries to work together. Türkiye’s goal is net-zero emissions by 2053.
content.transferTask: Write about why countries should work together for nature.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect the Green Deal with Türkiye’s own plan?

exitTicket: Write one sentence that starts with “In conclusion”.

metadata.title: The European Green Deal B1 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Our World Today
metadata.estimatedDuration: 8 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow connected informational texts about society, economy and the environment, and who can produce supported explanations and short arguments.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through an informational text about the European Green Deal: its aims and targets, the energy problem, renewable energy, the net-zero age, new rules, consumers and jobs, education and Türkiye’s own plan, using the Language Focus attached to every chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 8 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a picture of a label or a machine, or a link to the previous chapter.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: a definition map, three aims, a cause–result chain, a problem–solution chart, a future map, a rule chart or a two-part organizer.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets, Key Terms and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the chapter sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practice it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: a plan to / its aim is to + verb · by + -ing (method) · in this way
Ch2: reduce by + amount · by + deadline · without + -ing
Ch3: because · for this reason · as a result · present perfect (have affected)
Ch4: so that + can (purpose) · should (advice) · quit + -ing
Ch5: will (prediction) · can (possibility) · defining relative clauses (that / who / whose)
Ch6: be (not) allowed to · no longer · will need to
Ch7: depend on · instead of · help + person + base verb · compete for
Ch8: in conclusion · for this reason · it is helpful for … to · depend on how well

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, facts, numbers and arguments.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify main ideas, targets, causes, results and solutions.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: explain ideas, give reasons and propose solutions.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce connected B1 paragraphs using evidence, linking words and chapter patterns.

valuesFocus: D16 Responsibility — Caring for nature and our shared world.
D5 Sensitivity — Noticing what nature and people need.
D20 Helpfulness — Working together for a common goal.
D1 Justice — A fair change that protects everyone.
languageFocus: Every one of the 8 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the thinking target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, picture cards, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for one more sentence or one more reason from the book, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside numbers or opinions.
The book is about EU policy; Türkiye’s own plan (2021, net zero by 2053) is in Chapter 8. Present both as the book gives them.
Discuss energy and money at home with care; some families may have difficulties paying their bills.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The Green Deal connects with questions every community faces today: how to use less energy, how to protect nature and how to work together across borders.

themes.title: No borders:
themes.description: Climate change does not stop at borders (Chapter 8). Discuss why countries need to work together.

themes.title: Use less, repair more:
themes.description: In a circular economy, people recycle materials and produce less waste (Chapter 1). Discuss how families can waste less.

themes.title: Smart consumers:
themes.description: Consumers need clear information to make eco-friendly choices (Chapter 7). Discuss how labels help people in different countries.

themes.title: New skills:
themes.description: Workers at all levels need new skills (Chapter 7). Discuss which skills young people will need.

actions: Find the energy label on a machine at home and read it.
Repair or reuse one old thing this week.
Find Türkiye’s Green Deal Action Plan goal year on a class poster.

exitTicket: One idea from today’s chapter, with the sentence that supports it, is …
One language pattern I noticed today, and what it does in the sentence, is …
One action I can take this week for a greener world is …

miniProject.title: The Green Deal: A Class Summit
miniProject.desc: In groups, each member becomes an expert on two chapters: aims, energy, industry or people. Teach your part, then write a class declaration with four promises.

reflectivePrompt.title: A Green Future
reflectivePrompt.desc: Climate change does not stop at borders (Chapter 8). Write six to eight sentences about your community in a net-zero future.

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D16 Responsibility
items.value: Responsibility: The Green Deal wants people to benefit from nature responsibly (Chapter 2).

items.label: D5 Sensitivity
items.value: Sensitivity: Consumers should choose green products instead of products that cause a lot of pollution (Chapter 7).

items.label: D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Helpfulness: Climate change does not stop at borders, so it is helpful for countries to keep working together (Chapter 8).

items.label: D1 Justice
items.value: Justice: Education is important for a fair change that protects everyone (Chapter 8).

questions: What small action can show it this week?
Which part is from the book and which part is my own idea?

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR B1. The table links the B1 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test B1 to the chapters of this book where learners practice them.

rows.descriptor: Can read straightforward factual texts on subjects related to his/her field and interest with a satisfactory level of comprehension.
practice: Chapter 3 (Why Is the Green Deal Important?): Follow the cause–result chain.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write straightforward connected texts on a range of familiar subjects within his field of interest, by linking a series of shorter discrete elements into a linear sequence.
practice: Chapter 6 (New Rules for Green Products): Propose a new green rule.
Chapter 8 (Education and Working Together): Write about why countries should work together.
Language Review, “Use: A Green Future”: Write six to eight sentences.

rows.descriptor: Can reasonably fluently sustain a straightforward description of one of a variety of subjects within his/her field of interest, presenting it as a linear sequence of points.
practice: Chapter 4 (Moving to Renewable Energy): Give advice for a greener school.
Chapter 8 (Education and Working Together): Present your expert part in the class summit.

test.title: End-of-Level Test B1
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B1 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 70 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (45 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (25 minutes): on paper. Write an article for your school website about a person you admire. (100–130 words)
Speaking (about 8 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

content.chapter: Chapter 1: A Plan for a Greener Europe
objectives: I can explain what the Green Deal is and what it aims to do.
I can explain how a circular economy protects nature.
I can use purpose forms: a plan to, its aim is to, in this way.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “Its aim is to protect the planet by building a clean economy”: aim and method. Then choose the forms and rewrite three sentences.
content.lessonPlan: What does sustainable mean to you? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find the aim of the Green Deal. Make a definition map.
discussionPoints: A circular economy produces less waste. Which thing at home could you reuse instead of throwing away?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “11 December 2019” and “Less Waste” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the third sentence again. Find “Its aim is”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write four to five sentences about how your home could be more circular.

whatToNotice: The Green Deal is a plan for sustainable growth.
A circular economy produces less waste.
readListen: What does sustainable mean to you? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find the aim of the Green Deal.
Make a definition map.
findAnswerInStory: Find who announced the Green Deal and when.
Find the 2050 aim.
Find how nature is protected in a circular economy.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: sustainable, economy, greenhouse gas, emissions, eco-friendly, circular economy.
“In a sustainable way.” What does sustainable mean?
Write one sentence with emissions.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose the aim of the Green Deal. Read the third sentence.

metadata.title: The European Green Deal B1 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 25 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B1 learners who study the text about the European Green Deal alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 8 chapters of The European Green Deal.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Explain the aims, targets and rules of the Green Deal.
Explain the role of energy, consumers, education and cooperation with evidence from the book.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 8.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One idea from the Green Deal that I would like to remember:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 8 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 25 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows responsibility, sensitivity, helpfulness and justice. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Responsibility: Responsibility: The Green Deal wants people to benefit from nature responsibly (Chapter 2).
Sensitivity: Sensitivity: Consumers should choose green products instead of products that cause a lot of pollution (Chapter 7).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: Climate change does not stop at borders, so it is helpful for countries to keep working together (Chapter 8).
Justice: Justice: Education is important for a fair change that protects everyone (Chapter 8).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 8, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Key Facts
Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Key Terms
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell someone at home in five sentences what the Green Deal is and why it matters, in your home language or in English.
